Certified type:
- category: "Indicator"
- type_designations: ["IT9-AC", "IT9-DC"]
- module_designation: The characteristics mention "Configuration: Analog load cells", "Analog load cells with zener barriers", "Digital load cells or weighing module". Hmm, for an indicator, the module_designation is usually about the instrument module. The cert covers configurations with analog load cells, analog with zener barriers, digital load cells. This is more of a config-level thing. I'll set module_designation to null or maybe not applicable. Actually, for indicators, there isn't a module designation like "Analog load cell" for the certified type itself. I'll omit or null. Maybe null.

- description: null / omit

model_family: The cert covers 2 model variants: IT9-AC and IT9-DC. Should I include model_family? Rule says include ONLY if cert covers >1 model variant. There are two types: IT9-AC and IT9-DC. The characteristics don't vary by model in tables though — the tables vary by configuration (analog load cells, analog with zener barriers, digital load cells). So maybe I should list models IT9-AC and IT9-DC in model_family but there are no model-level attributes. Alternatively, could treat them as models with no distinguishing attributes. The rule says "include ONLY if cert covers >1 model variant" — there are 2 type designations. I think it's safe to include model_family with models [{"model_id": "IT9-AC"}, {"model_id": "IT9-DC"}] and family_name null.

Actually, the differences between IT9-AC and IT9-DC might relate to power supply: AC (100-240V AC) vs DC (12-24V DC). The power supply characteristic says "100 – 240 V AC 50/60 Hz or 12 – 24 V DC (suitable for road vehicle power supply)". That could map: IT9-AC → AC power, IT9-DC → DC power. But that's inference; don't fabricate. I'll just list the models without attributes, or maybe put power supply in type_level as it applies to all.

Components: The indicator itself is the certified type. No sub-assemblies named other than configurations. I might not include components.

Characteristics: The tables describe three configurations:
1. Analog load cells (page 2)
2. Analog load cells with zener barriers on the load cell interface (page 3, first table)
3. Digital load cells or weighing module (page 3, second table)
Plus page 4: All configurations — temperature range, mechanical environment class, electromagnetic environment class, power supply voltage.

This is a config-level structure: attribute varies by configuration. Use characteristics.config_level with axis = "load cell interface configuration" (or "configuration").

Config-level entries:

attribute: maximum_number_of_scale_intervals
axis: configuration
values:
- {condition: "Analog load cells, without overvoltage protection on the load cell interface", value: {max: 10000, min: null}? Actually "n ≤ 10000". Value is a max bound: value 10000 with the attribute being "maximum number of scale intervals". Hmm, how to encode "n ≤ 10000"? The attribute is already "maximum number of scale intervals" so value: 10000 makes sense. But rule about structured values: value must be object with value/unit etc. The config_level entries: "Values follow the same structured form: {condition, value, unit_symbol}". So value can be number 10000.

But the table distinguishes "Without overvoltage protection on the load cell interface" (n ≤ 10000) vs "With overvoltage protection" (n ≤ 8750) for analog config. That's a sub-condition. So for config "Analog load cells" there are two sub-conditions. I could encode:

config_level entry:
- attribute: "maximum_number_of_scale_intervals"
  axis: "configuration"
  values: [
    {condition: "analog_load_cells_without_overvoltage_protection", value: 10000, unit_symbol: null},
    {condition: "analog_load_cells_with_overvoltage_protection", value: 8750, unit_symbol: null},
    {condition: "analog_load_cells_with_zener_barriers", value: 6000, unit_symbol: null},
    {condition: "digital_load_cells_or_weighing_module", value: "equal to the maximum number of scale intervals of the digital load cell or weighing module", unit_symbol: null}
  ]

Alternatively encode the overvoltage as a second axis. The schema allows only one axis per entry, but I can create multiple entries. Perhaps simpler: define axis as "configuration" with conditions describing config and sub-condition textually.

Let me enumerate all characteristics per configuration:

- maximum number of load platforms: 8

Config B: "Analog load cells with zener barriers on the load cell interface"

- weighing ranges: single, multi-interval, multiple range

- max load cell resistance: 3300 Ω

Config C: "Digital load cells or weighing module"

- weighing ranges: single, multi, multiple range

All configs:

- electromagnetic environment class: E3
- power supply voltage: 100–240 V AC 50/60 Hz or 12–24 V DC

Per rule 3, power supply: split into power_supply_voltage (AC: 100-240 V; DC: 12-24 V), power_supply_frequency (50-60 Hz), power_supply_type AC/DC.

  - power_supply_voltage: maybe two entries? Schema says type_level: <label>: {value, unit_symbol, ...} single value per label.   - note: suitable for road vehicle power supply (DC). Maybe as a description note; could add footnote? Not a footnote. I could include in description or skip. I'll add a note in power_supply_voltage_dc? The schema is strict: {value, unit_symbol, footnote_markers}. Maybe add "power_supply_note": {value: "suitable for road vehicle power supply (12–24 V DC)"}. Hmm, might be noisy. I'll include a note characteristic? I think it's fine to include it as a string value characteristic "power_supply_dc_note". Or skip. I'll include it as "suitable_for_road_vehicle_power_supply": {value: true}? That may be over-engineering. I'll include "power_supply_dc_note": value string. Actually simpler: omit; not essential. But "don't fabricate" only means don't invent; including is optional. I'll include a compact note.

Config-level entries (axis: "configuration" with conditions):

   - condition "Analog load cells": value "(III) or (IIII)"
   - condition "Analog load cells with zener barriers": value "(III) or (IIII)"

   Hmm, the sub-conditions again. Actually for zener config the table only gives one value: 5782.5. It doesn't say whether with/without OVP. I'll use condition "Analog load cells with zener barriers".

   unit "m/mm²" is weird (m·mm⁻²? Actually cable length per cross-section unit is m/mm²). Keep unit_symbol "m/mm²".

Structured value format: In the schema example at top: `characteristics: type_level: <label>: {value, unit_symbol, footnote_markers[]}`. And rule 3 examples show `value: {min, max}, unit_symbol: "°C"`. So each value object: {"value": ..., "unit_symbol": ..., "unit_id": null, "footnote_markers": []}. Should I include unit_id and footnote_markers always? Rule 2 says every characteristic value MUST be an object with that shape. I'll include unit_id: null and footnote_markers only when present (or empty array). To be safe include unit_id null; footnote_markers omit unless present? The shape includes footnote_markers; I'll include empty arrays for consistency, or omit when empty. The schema shape shows footnote_markers: ["1)"]. I'll include footnote_markers only when non-empty to reduce noise. Hmm, "MUST be an object with this shape" — includes footnote_markers. I'll include footnote_markers: [] everywhere for compliance. That's a lot of repetition but fine.

Actually, to keep JSON manageable, I'll include footnote_markers only where applicable. The instruction says the shape includes it, but omitting empty fields is generally acceptable ("If a field is not present in the markdown, omit it" — rule 8). I'll omit empty footnote_markers and unit_id when null? Rule 2 shows unit_id in the shape. Hmm. I'll include "unit_id": null for entries that have unit_symbol, and omit both unit_id and footnote_markers when there is no unit/footnote. Actually simpler and safer: include unit_symbol when present, omit unit_id (always null, no certainty) — but rule 3 says "Leave unit_id: null unless you are certain". Leaving null means the key exists with null. I'll include "unit_id": null consistently. And footnote_markers only when present. Let me just include both keys always with defaults (unit_id: null, footnote_markers: []). It's verbose but compliant.

Hmm, this JSON will get long. Let's be pragmatic: include unit_id: null and footnote_markers: [] on all value objects.
